claim: Listeners were more accurate to detect source appearance in scenes comprised of temporally-regular (REG), rather than random (RAND), sources.
source: Listeners were more accurate and quicker to detect source apperance when the scene structure was temporally regular (REG) versus random (RAND; d' F(1,12) = 100.7, p<0.001; detection times F(1,12) = 17.61, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data showing significant difference in d' scores between REG and RAND conditions

claim: Listeners were quicker to detect source appearance in scenes comprised of temporally-regular (REG), rather than random (RAND), sources.
source: Listeners were more accurate and quicker to detect source apperance when the scene structure was temporally regular (REG) versus random (RAND; d' F(1,12) = 100.7, p<0.001; detection times F(1,12) = 17.61, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data showing significant difference in detection times between REG and RAND conditions

claim: The effect of scene temporal structure on detection performance occurred independently of the temporal structure of the appearing component.
source: This effect occurred independently of the temporal structure of the appearing component (d' F(1,12) = 0.075, p=0.789; detection times F(1,12) = 4.23, p=0.062).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no significant interaction between scene structure and appearing source structure

claim: Listeners were quicker (by ~27 ms) to detect source appearance when it was temporally regular.
source: Additionally, listeners were quicker (by ~27 ms) to detect source appearance when it was temporally regular (detection times F(1,12) = 5.70, p<0.050), although this effect did not extend to d' (F(1,12) = 2.29, p=0.156).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of detection times showing significant effect of appearing source temporal structure

claim: The mean hit rate was high (mean = 76.1%, ranging from 57 to 97% across listeners).
source: Overall, the mean hit rate was high (mean = 76.1%, ranging from 57 to 97% across listeners) and mean false alarm rate low (mean = 6.25%, ranging from 0 to 18.8%).
evidence: Supported by descriptive statistics of behavioral performance

claim: The mean false alarm rate was low (mean = 6.25%, ranging from 0 to 18.8%).
source: Overall, the mean hit rate was high (mean = 76.1%, ranging from 57 to 97% across listeners) and mean false alarm rate low (mean = 6.25%, ranging from 0 to 18.8%).
evidence: Supported by descriptive statistics of behavioral performance

claim: The neural response evoked by scene onset is characterized by a series of deflections at around 80, 110 and 200 ms.
source: The neural response evoked by scene onset (i.e. prior to any scene change) is characterized by a series of deflections at around 80, 110 and 200 ms, with topographies corresponding to the commonly observed M50, M100 and M200 onset-response components (Eggermont and Ponton, 2002).
evidence: Supported by MEG data analysis and cited reference to established components

claim: The scene-evoked response deflections correspond to the commonly observed M50, M100 and M200 onset-response components.
source: The neural response evoked by scene onset (i.e. prior to any scene change) is characterized by a series of deflections at around 80, 110 and 200 ms, with topographies corresponding to the commonly observed M50, M100 and M200 onset-response components (Eggermont and Ponton, 2002).
evidence: Supported by comparison to established literature on auditory evoked responses

claim: From around 300 ms post onset, the scene-evoked response settles to a sustained amplitude.
source: From around 300 ms post onset, the response settles to a sustained amplitude.
evidence: Supported by MEG data analysis showing temporal dynamics of the response

claim: Scene temporal structure had a significant effect on the evoked response from 436 ms in the Passive group.
source: Scene temporal structure had a significant effect on the evoked response from 436 ms in the Passive group and from 476 ms in the Active group, involving an increase in the sustained response for REG versus RAND conditions (temporal clusters with FWE corrected significance are indicated as thick horizontal green bars in Figure 2; uncorrected clusters are shown as thin light-green bars).
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: Scene temporal structure had a significant effect on the evoked response from 476 ms in the Active group.
source: Scene temporal structure had a significant effect on the evoked response from 436 ms in the Passive group and from 476 ms in the Active group, involving an increase in the sustained response for REG versus RAND conditions (temporal clusters with FWE corrected significance are indicated as thick horizontal green bars in Figure 2; uncorrected clusters are shown as thin light-green bars).
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: Scene temporal structure effects involved an increase in the sustained response for REG versus RAND conditions.
source: Scene temporal structure had a significant effect on the evoked response from 436 ms in the Passive group and from 476 ms in the Active group, involving an increase in the sustained response for REG versus RAND conditions (temporal clusters with FWE corrected significance are indicated as thick horizontal green bars in Figure 2; uncorrected clusters are shown as thin light-green bars).
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: The topographical patterns for REG and RAND conditions (averaged over the 500–800 ms period of the sustained response) were qualitatively similar in both Passive and Active groups.
source: The topographical patterns for REG and RAND conditions (averaged over the 500–800 ms period of the sustained response) were qualitatively similar in both Passive and Active groups (also shown in Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of topographical maps in Figure 2

claim: The mean onset latency of the scene structure effect was 289 ms for Passive group.
source: Mean onset latencies for each group are shown as vertical purple lines in Figure 2 (289 ms for Passive; 412 ms for Active).
evidence: Supported by jackknife resampling procedure on MEG data

claim: The mean onset latency of the scene structure effect was 412 ms for Active group.
source: Mean onset latencies for each group are shown as vertical purple lines in Figure 2 (289 ms for Passive; 412 ms for Active).
evidence: Supported by jackknife resampling procedure on MEG data

claim: The scene structure effect emerged on average 123 ms earlier in the Passive versus Active groups.
source: Although the scene structure effect emerged on average, 123 ms earlier in the Passive versus Active groups, there was no significant difference in onset latency between groups (jackknife adjusted two-sample t(25) = −1.35, p=0.188).
evidence: Supported by jackknife resampling procedure comparing onset latencies between groups

claim: There was no significant difference in onset latency of the scene structure effect between Passive and Active groups.
source: Although the scene structure effect emerged on average, 123 ms earlier in the Passive versus Active groups, there was no significant difference in onset latency between groups (jackknife adjusted two-sample t(25) = −1.35, p=0.188).
evidence: Supported by statistical test on jackknife-estimated latencies

claim: There was no main effect of group on the magnitude of the sustained response.
source: Neither was there a main effect of group (p=0.48) or scene structure by group interaction (p=0.31) when conducting ANOVA on the magnitude of the sustained response (averaged from 500–800 ms).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA on MEG data

claim: There was no scene structure by group interaction on the magnitude of the sustained response.
source: Neither was there a main effect of group (p=0.48) or scene structure by group interaction (p=0.31) when conducting ANOVA on the magnitude of the sustained response (averaged from 500–800 ms).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA on MEG data

claim: The scene-evoked response showed no evidence of attentional modulation during the M50, M100 and M200 components.
source: This was also the case for earlier time-windows during the M50, M100 and M200 components (all p's >0.19).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MEG data at early time windows

claim: Regular scene structure results in an increased MEG response from around 400 ms post scene onset.
source: In summary, when MEG responses are timelocked to scene onset, regular scene structure results in an increased MEG response from around 400 ms post scene onset.
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: The scene-evoked response shows no evidence of attentional modulation in terms of an overall difference between Passive and Active groups.
source: Furthermore, the scene-evoked response shows no evidence of attentional modulation, either in terms of an overall difference between Passive and Active groups or the interaction between scene structure and group.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no main effect of group

claim: The scene-evoked response shows no evidence of attentional modulation in terms of the interaction between scene structure and group.
source: Furthermore, the scene-evoked response shows no evidence of attentional modulation, either in terms of an overall difference between Passive and Active groups or the interaction between scene structure and group.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no interaction effect

claim: The appearance-evoked responses are characterized by later latencies (around 90, 150 and 300 ms, respectively) than those typically observed in other studies.
source: Although the responses here are characterized by later latencies (around 90, 150 and 300 ms, respectively) than those typically observed in other studies that report similar deflections.
evidence: Supported by comparison of observed latencies to literature

claim: The delayed appearance-evoked responses may be due to the higher complexity of the present stimuli.
source: This may be due to the higher complexity of the present stimuli, which is known to lead to delayed responses (see e.g. Chait et al., 2008; Sohoglu and Chait, 2016).
evidence: Supported by inference from cited literature on stimulus complexity effects

claim: M50 and M200 deflections are observed in the Passive group.
source: M50 and M200 deflections are also observed in the Passive group but we note with interest the absence of a prominent M100 component, consistent with previous reports of this component being particularly sensitive to attention and/or task-related demands (Ahveninen et al., 2011; Ding and Simon, 2012; Königs and Gutschalk, 2012; Sohoglu and Chait, 2016).
evidence: Supported by MEG data analysis in Passive group

claim: There is an absence of a prominent M100 component in the Passive group.
source: M50 and M200 deflections are also observed in the Passive group but we note with interest the absence of a prominent M100 component, consistent with previous reports of this component being particularly sensitive to attention and/or task-related demands (Ahveninen et al., 2011; Ding and Simon, 2012; Königs and Gutschalk, 2012; Sohoglu and Chait, 2016).
evidence: Supported by MEG data analysis and comparison to cited literature

claim: The M100 component is particularly sensitive to attention and/or task-related demands.
source: M50 and M200 deflections are also observed in the Passive group but we note with interest the absence of a prominent M100 component, consistent with previous reports of this component being particularly sensitive to attention and/or task-related demands (Ahveninen et al., 2011; Ding and Simon, 2012; Königs and Gutschalk, 2012; Sohoglu and Chait, 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited literature on M100 component properties

claim: Scene structure had a significant effect on the appearance-evoked response from 96 ms in the Passive group.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, cluster-based statistics showed a significant effect of scene structure on the appearance-evoked response from 96 ms in the Passive group and from 260 ms in the Active group, both involving an increased neural response for REG versus RAND conditions.
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: Scene structure had a significant effect on the appearance-evoked response from 260 ms in the Active group.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, cluster-based statistics showed a significant effect of scene structure on the appearance-evoked response from 96 ms in the Passive group and from 260 ms in the Active group, both involving an increased neural response for REG versus RAND conditions.
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: The scene structure effect on appearance-evoked response involved an increased neural response for REG versus RAND conditions in both Passive and Active groups.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, cluster-based statistics showed a significant effect of scene structure on the appearance-evoked response from 96 ms in the Passive group and from 260 ms in the Active group, both involving an increased neural response for REG versus RAND conditions.
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: The scene structure effect was apparent in the Passive group already at the earliest M50 component.
source: This effect was apparent in the Passive group already at the earliest M50 component while in the Active group, it was confined to later components of the evoked response (M200 at corrected significance; M100 uncorrected).
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: In the Active group, the scene structure effect was confined to later components of the evoked response (M200 at corrected significance; M100 uncorrected).
source: This effect was apparent in the Passive group already at the earliest M50 component while in the Active group, it was confined to later components of the evoked response (M200 at corrected significance; M100 uncorrected).
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on MEG data

claim: The topographical patterns for REG and RAND conditions in the appearance-evoked response were qualitatively similar in both Passive and Active groups.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, the topographical patterns for REG and RAND conditions were qualitatively similar in both Passive and Active groups.
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of topographical maps in Figure 3A

claim: The measured effect of REG versus RAND on appearance-evoked response is distinct to that observed for the scene-evoked response.
source: As described previously, the appearance-evoked response was derived by baseline correcting relative to the 200 ms period prior to source appearance and therefore the measured effect of REG versus RAND is distinct to that observed for the scene-evoked response.
evidence: Supported by methodological description of baseline correction procedure

claim: For matched trials in which there was no change (no appearing source), no effect of REG versus RAND was observed.
source: To confirm this, we also analyzed matched trials in which there was no change (no appearing source; shown as transparent traces in Figure 3A). For this analysis, no effect of REG versus RAND was observed, confirming that scene structure modulates the appearance-evoked response in addition to the scene-evoked response.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of no-change trials

claim: Scene structure modulates the appearance-evoked response in addition to the scene-evoked response.
source: To confirm this, we also analyzed matched trials in which there was no change (no appearing source; shown as transparent traces in Figure 3A). For this analysis, no effect of REG versus RAND was observed, confirming that scene structure modulates the appearance-evoked response in addition to the scene-evoked response.
evidence: Supported by comparison of appearance trials and no-change trials

claim: The scene structure effect occurred on average 55 ms earlier in Passive versus Active groups.
source: The scene structure effect was estimated to occur on average, 55 ms earlier in Passive versus Active groups (mean onset latency = 87 ms for Passive; 142 ms for Active).
evidence: Supported by jackknife resampling procedure on appearance-evoked MEG data

claim: The mean onset latency of the scene structure effect on appearance-evoked response was 87 ms for Passive group.
source: The scene structure effect was estimated to occur on average, 55 ms earlier in Passive versus Active groups (mean onset latency = 87 ms for Passive; 142 ms for Active).
evidence: Supported by jackknife resampling procedure on MEG data

claim: The mean onset latency of the scene structure effect on appearance-evoked response was 142 ms for Active group.
source: The scene structure effect was estimated to occur on average, 55 ms earlier in Passive versus Active groups (mean onset latency = 87 ms for Passive; 142 ms for Active).
evidence: Supported by jackknife resampling procedure on MEG data

claim: The difference in onset latency of the scene structure effect between Passive and Active groups was confirmed significant.
source: This difference was confirmed significant using a jackknife adjusted independent samples test (t(25) = −3.96, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical test on jackknife-estimated latencies

claim: The difference in MEG response between REG and RAND conditions at the time of the appearance-evoked M50 (72–112 ms) was significantly stronger in Passive versus Active groups.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the difference in MEG response between REG and RAND conditions was significantly stronger in Passive versus Active groups (t(25) = 1.78, p<0.05.).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc between-group t-test on MEG data

claim: Despite listeners' detection times being somewhat quicker when the appearing source was temporally regular versus random (by ~27 ms on average), no significant differences in MEG response were observed in Passive or Active groups.
source: Despite listeners' detection times being somewhat quicker when the appearing source was temporally regular versus random (by ~27 ms on average across the group; shown earlier in Figure 1B), no significant differences in MEG response were observed in Passive or Active groups.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MEG data as a function of appearing source structure

claim: There was no significant interaction between scene and appearing source structure on MEG response.
source: Neither was there a significant interaction between scene and appearing source structure.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MEG data

claim: The scene-evoked response (averaged from 500 to 800 ms) showed greater source power for REG versus RAND scenes in both hemispheres of the superior temporal lobe, including primary auditory cortex, planum temporale and the superior temporal gyrus.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, the scene-evoked response (averaged from 500 to 800 ms) showed greater source power for REG versus RAND scenes in both hemispheres of the superior temporal lobe, including primary auditory cortex, planum temporale and the superior temporal gyrus (peak voxel locations are reported in Table 1).
evidence: Supported by source reconstruction analysis of MEG data

claim: An additional distinct cluster of activation for the scene-evoked response is observed in left post central gyrus of the superior parietal lobe.
source: An additional distinct cluster of activation is observed in left post central gyrus of the superior parietal lobe.
evidence: Supported by source reconstruction analysis of MEG data

claim: The scene structure by group interaction ([REG>RAND] > [Passive>Active]) during the early M50 component localized to superior/middle temporal lobe (in the right hemisphere only) and post central gyrus.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, this effect localized to similar regions as for the scene-evoked response: superior/middle temporal lobe (albeit in the right hemisphere only) and post central gyrus.
evidence: Supported by source reconstruction analysis of MEG data

claim: Additional activation for the appearance-evoked interaction is observed more anteriorly in the pre central gyrus, extending into the middle frontal gyrus.
source: Additional activation is observed more anteriorly in the pre central gyrus, extending into the middle frontal gyrus.
evidence: Supported by source reconstruction analysis of MEG data

claim: Listeners' ability to detect the appearance of a new source was enhanced in temporally regular scenes.
source: We demonstrate that listeners' ability to detect the appearance of a new source was enhanced in temporally regular scenes.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing improved detection performance in REG versus RAND scenes

claim: Behavioral benefits of statistical structure on scene analysis are associated with increased neural responses occurring before as well as after source appearance.
source: These behavioral benefits of statistical structure on scene analysis are associated with increased neural responses occurring before as well as after source appearance.
evidence: Supported by MEG data showing increased responses for REG scenes both in scene-evoked and appearance-evoked analyses

claim: Around 400 ms following scene onset, there was an increase in the sustained MEG response for scenes consisting of regularly structured, relative to randomly fluctuating sources.
source: Around 400 ms following scene onset, we observed an increase in the sustained MEG response for scenes consisting of regularly structured, relative to randomly fluctuating sources.
evidence: Supported by MEG data analysis showing sustained response differences

claim: The finding of increased sustained MEG response for regular scenes is opposite to what would be expected based on adaptation.
source: This finding is opposite to what would be expected based on adaptation i.e. decreased neural responses for temporally regular events, which has previously been observed for isolated tone sequences (Costa-Faidella et al., 2011; Schwartze et al., 2013; Tavano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by comparison to cited literature on adaptation effects

claim: Decreased neural responses for temporally regular events have previously been observed for isolated tone sequences.
source: This finding is opposite to what would be expected based on adaptation i.e. decreased neural responses for temporally regular events, which has previously been observed for isolated tone sequences (Costa-Faidella et al., 2011; Schwartze et al., 2013; Tavano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature on adaptation

claim: The increased sustained response for regular scenes is consistent with a mechanism that infers the precision (predictability) of sensory input and uses this information to up-regulate neural processing towards more reliable sensory signals.
source: It is however consistent with a mechanism that infers the precision (predictability) of sensory input and uses this information to up-regulate neural processing towards more reliable sensory signals (Feldman and Friston, 2010; Zhao et al., 2013; Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2015; Barascud et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by comparison to theoretical framework in cited literature

claim: The magnitude of sustained MEG activity (from naïve distracted listeners) tracks the predictability of rapid tone sequences.
source: Indeed, it has recently been demonstrated that the magnitude of sustained MEG activity (from naïve distracted listeners) tracks the predictability of rapid tone sequences (Barascud et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: In Barascud et al. (2016), regularity was characterized by a spectral pattern repeating over time within a single ongoing tone sequence.
source: In that study, regularity was characterized by a spectral pattern repeating over time within a single ongoing tone sequence.
evidence: Supported by description of cited study

claim: The ensuing effect on MEG response in Barascud et al. (2016) is strikingly similar to the sustained effect observed in the current study.
source: Although distinct to the temporal regularity studied here, the ensuing effect on MEG response is strikingly similar to the sustained effect we observe.
evidence: Supported by comparison of current findings to cited study

claim: The current findings demonstrate mechanisms that automatically (irrespective of directed attention) and rapidly (within 400 ms of scene onset) encode regularities distributed over many concurrent sources.
source: Importantly, the current findings demonstrate mechanisms that automatically (irrespective of directed attention) and rapidly (within 400 ms of scene onset) encode regularities distributed over many concurrent sources, typical of natural listening environments.
evidence: Supported by MEG data showing scene structure effects in both Passive and Active groups

claim: The MEG response in naïve, passively listening subjects revealed a large (22%) increase in the evoked response starting from the very first response deflection (M50 component) following source appearance.
source: The MEG response in naïve, passively listening subjects revealed a large (22%) increase in the evoked response starting from the very first response deflection (M50 component) following source appearance.
evidence: Supported by MEG data analysis in Passive group

claim: The increased appearance-evoked response for REG scenes occurred over and above that observed prior to the appearance event.
source: Importantly, this effect occurred over and above that observed prior to the appearance event, demonstrating bottom-up driven 'surprise' responses tightly linked to the predictability of the ongoing scene context.
evidence: Supported by baseline-corrected MEG analysis showing appearance-specific effects

claim: The increased appearance-evoked response for REG scenes demonstrates bottom-up driven 'surprise' responses tightly linked to the predictability of the ongoing scene context.
source: Importantly, this effect occurred over and above that observed prior to the appearance event, demonstrating bottom-up driven 'surprise' responses tightly linked to the predictability of the ongoing scene context.
evidence: Supported by MEG data showing appearance-specific effects and theoretical interpretation

claim: The REG>RAND effect on appearance-evoked response emerged substantially later when participants were actively attending to the appearance events.
source: Interestingly, the REG>RAND effect emerged substantially later when participants were actively attending to the appearance events.
evidence: Supported by comparison of onset latencies between Passive and Active groups

claim: The enhanced detection performance observed in behavior is not solely the result of changes in neural responses occurring prior to source appearance.
source: Overall, the results demonstrate that the enhanced detection performance observed in behavior is not solely the result of changes in neural responses occurring prior to source appearance (cf. adaptation accounts; May et al., 1999; Jääskeläinen et al., 2004) but also due to enhanced neural responses to novel events themselves.
evidence: Supported by MEG data showing both scene-evoked and appearance-evoked effects

claim: The enhanced detection performance is also due to enhanced neural responses to novel events themselves.
source: Overall, the results demonstrate that the enhanced detection performance observed in behavior is not solely the result of changes in neural responses occurring prior to source appearance (cf. adaptation accounts; May et al., 1999; Jääskeläinen et al., 2004) but also due to enhanced neural responses to novel events themselves.
evidence: Supported by MEG data showing increased appearance-evoked responses for REG scenes

claim: The pattern of results is what would be expected based on precision accounts.
source: This is again what would be expected based on precision accounts and is also consistent with animal physiology work showing that the magnitude of responses in single neurons of auditory cortex to new ('deviant') tones is larger than expected based on simple adaptation to previously repeated ('standard') tones alone (Khouri and Nelken, 2015).
evidence: Supported by comparison to theoretical framework and cited animal physiology work

claim: The magnitude of responses in single neurons of auditory cortex to new ('deviant') tones is larger than expected based on simple adaptation to previously repeated ('standard') tones alone.
source: This is again what would be expected based on precision accounts and is also consistent with animal physiology work showing that the magnitude of responses in single neurons of auditory cortex to new ('deviant') tones is larger than expected based on simple adaptation to previously repeated ('standard') tones alone (Khouri and Nelken, 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited animal physiology work

claim: Neural responses in a network of brain regions are modulated by scene temporal structure, including early auditory regions in the superior temporal lobe and left parietal cortex (post central gyrus).
source: Source reconstruction suggests that neural responses in a network of brain regions are modulated by scene temporal structure, including early auditory regions in the superior temporal lobe but also left parietal cortex (post central gyrus).
evidence: Supported by source reconstruction analysis of MEG data

claim: Left parietal cortex has a specific role in temporal processing.
source: This is consistent with evidence from neuroimaging (Rao et al., 2001; Coull and Nobre, 2008; Andreou et al., 2015), electrophysiology (Leon et al., 2003; Janssen and Shadlen, 2005) and lesion studies (Harrington et al., 1998; Battelli et al., 2008) implicating a specific role for left parietal cortex in temporal processing.
evidence: Supported by cited literature from multiple methodologies

claim: Parietal cortex has been associated with figure-ground processing when the figure is defined by temporally repeatable spectral components in an otherwise randomly structured background.
source: Parietal cortex has also been associated with figure-ground processing when the figure is defined by temporally repeatable spectral components in an otherwise randomly structured background (Teki et al., 2011; Teki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Parietal cortex may be part of a wider network (along with auditory cortical regions) that codes the temporal structure of acoustic scenes.
source: Thus, together the current study and previous findings suggest parietal cortex may be part of a wider network (along with auditory cortical regions) that codes the temporal structure of acoustic scenes.
evidence: Supported by integration of current findings with cited literature

claim: The parietal activity changes may reflect a more domain-general increase in bottom-up saliency attributable to regularity.
source: Alternatively, the parietal activity changes we observe may reflect a more domain-general increase in bottom-up saliency attributable to regularity (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by alternative theoretical interpretation based on cited literature

claim: Barascud et al. (2016) did not observe changes in MEG and fMRI responses in parietal cortex for spectral regularity.
source: We note however that although Barascud et al. (2016) report effects of statistical structure in early auditory regions (like the current findings), they did not observe changes in MEG and fMRI responses in parietal cortex.
evidence: Supported by description of cited study

claim: In Barascud et al. (2016), spectral regularity modulated activity in the inferior frontal gyrus.
source: Instead, spectral regularity modulated activity in the inferior frontal gyrus.
evidence: Supported by description of cited study

claim: The difference in brain regions activated by temporal versus spectral regularity may suggest a degree of neural specialization for the particular type of regularity encoded.
source: This is may suggest a degree of neural specialization for the particular type of regularity encoded e.g. temporal-based involving parietal cortex versus spectral-based involving inferior frontal regions.
evidence: Supported by comparison of current findings to cited study and speculative interpretation

claim: Following scene onset (prior to new source appearance), the neural influence of regularity showed no evidence of attentional modulation.
source: Following scene onset (prior to new source appearance), the neural influence of regularity showed no evidence of attentional modulation (the strength of the scene-evoked response to regularly and randomly structured scenes was statistically indistinguishable in passive compared with active listening subjects).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no group differences or interactions

claim: The brain automatically encodes scene regularities, irrespective of directed attention.
source: This suggests that the brain automatically encodes scene regularities, irrespective of directed attention.
evidence: Supported by MEG data showing scene structure effects in both Passive and Active groups

claim: After the appearance of a new source, regularity and attention had an interactive influence on the evoked response.
source: After the appearance of a new source, however, regularity and attention had an interactive influence on the evoked response; whereas the first cortical deflection of the appearance-evoked response (M50) increased in regular scenes during passive listening, this effect was confined to later deflections (M100 and M200) when listeners actively detected source appearance.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing interaction between scene structure and group

claim: The first cortical deflection of the appearance-evoked response (M50) increased in regular scenes during passive listening.
source: After the appearance of a new source, however, regularity and attention had an interactive influence on the evoked response; whereas the first cortical deflection of the appearance-evoked response (M50) increased in regular scenes during passive listening, this effect was confined to later deflections (M100 and M200) when listeners actively detected source appearance.
evidence: Supported by MEG data analysis in Passive group

claim: The scene structure effect on appearance-evoked response was confined to later deflections (M100 and M200) when listeners actively detected source appearance.
source: After the appearance of a new source, however, regularity and attention had an interactive influence on the evoked response; whereas the first cortical deflection of the appearance-evoked response (M50) increased in regular scenes during passive listening, this effect was confined to later deflections (M100 and M200) when listeners actively detected source appearance.
evidence: Supported by MEG data analysis in Active group

claim: One proposal is that attention (like regularity) acts to determine the inferred precision of sensory input.
source: One proposal is that attention (like regularity) acts to determine the inferred precision of sensory input (Friston, 2009; Barascud et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited theoretical framework

claim: Attention increases precision (and neural responses) when sensory signals are task-relevant.
source: In this view, attention increases precision (and neural responses) when sensory signals are task-relevant.
evidence: Supported by description of theoretical framework

claim: Hsu et al. (2014) demonstrated greater EEG responses for predictable (ascending) pitch patterns, which was most apparent when those patterns were embedded in an attended stream.
source: Indeed, Hsu et al. (2014) demonstrated greater EEG responses for predictable (ascending) pitch patterns, which was most apparent when those patterns were embedded in an attended stream.
evidence: Supported by cited study

claim: Attention in the current study delayed the influence of regularity on appearance-related responses.
source: In contrast to this pattern, attention in our study delayed the influence of regularity on appearance-related responses.
evidence: Supported by comparison of onset latencies between Passive and Active groups

claim: When listeners actively detected source appearance, scene changes were relatively more expected.
source: We suggest that attention in our study acted as a form of expectation. That is, when listeners actively detected source appearance, scene changes were relatively more expected.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental design and task demands

claim: If change-related responses reflect the amount of 'surprise' given the preceding stimulus context, then they should diminish when change is expected and counteract the precision-mediated increase from regularity.
source: If change-related responses reflect the amount of 'surprise' given the preceding stimulus context, then they should diminish when change is expected and counteract the precision-mediated increase from regularity.
evidence: Supported by theoretical reasoning about surprise and expectation

claim: The later benefit from regularity when listeners are actively seeking source appearance is consistent with attention acting to reduce surprise.
source: Thus, although counterintuitive, the later benefit from regularity when listeners are actively seeking source appearance is consistent with attention acting to reduce surprise.
evidence: Supported by interpretation of MEG data in light of theoretical framework

claim: The mismatch negativity (MMN) response is often interpreted as reflecting 'surprise'.
source: In the auditory modality, the mismatch negativity (MMN) response is often interpreted as reflecting 'surprise' (Näätänen et al., 2007; Garrido et al., 2009).
